In [[representation theory]], a '''subrepresentation''' of a [[group representation|representation]] <math>(\pi, V)</math> of a [[group (mathematics)|group]] ''G'' is a representation <math>(\pi|_W, W)</math> such that ''W'' is a [[vector subspace]] of ''V'' and <math>\pi|_W(g) = \pi(g)|_W</math>.

A nonzero finite-dimensional representation always contains a nonzero subrepresentation that is [[irreducible representation|irreducible]], the fact seen by [[mathematical induction|induction]] on dimension. This fact is generally false for infinite-dimensional representations.

If <math>(\pi, V)</math> is a representation of ''G'', then there is the '''trivial subrepresentation''':
:<math>V^G = \{ v \in V \mid \pi(g)v = v, \, g \in G \}.</math>
If <math>f: V \to W </math> is an '''[[equivariant map]]''' between two representations, then its kernel is a subrepresentation of <math>V</math> and its image is a subrepresentation of <math>W</math>.
